subtype: Approach: contingency planning for illness or power cuts [Thinking]
passage: Shalini, beta, sit. You think your Nani never had exams? I am Sarita, and when I was sixteen in Nagpur, April meant two things: the light going off every evening and half the class down with fever. So I sat with my chart and thought, something will break, it always does. I had my notes photocopied and kept the printed set in a folder, so a dark room or a heavy head could not take them. And I left Sunday afternoons empty on purpose, one spare slot. My friend Leela laughed at those empty Sundays. In the third week the fever caught me for three days and the lights went twice. My Sunday was free, and I was caught up by evening. Leela came to my door that week, asking for the printed notes, because her house had no light.

qa.q: What did Sarita leave empty on purpose?
qa.a: Sarita left Sunday afternoons empty on purpose, one spare slot.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel about the chance of a disruption before it happened, and what shows it?
qa.a: Sarita felt realistic and prepared rather than panicked; expecting that 'something will break,' Sarita photocopied notes and kept a spare Sunday.

qa.q: Besides printed notes and an empty Sunday, what other approach could protect a student during a sick week, and why?
qa.a: Sarita could have asked a classmate to share the missed lesson notes, because one spare slot cannot cover a long illness by itself.

qa.q: How did Leela's view of the empty Sundays change?
qa.a: Leela first laughed at the empty Sundays, but when Leela's house had no light, Leela came asking for the printed notes and saw why they mattered.

grounding: Knowing summer power cuts and fevers are common, the student keeps printed notes and a spare Sunday slot so one disruption does not derail the schedule.

subtype: Approach: contingency planning for illness or power cuts [Thinking]
passage: Three weeks before her exams, Preeti sat with her study calendar and asked herself what usually went wrong in May in Lucknow. The power cuts, most evenings, sometimes for hours. And fevers: last year half her class went down with one. If the lights go, my laptop notes are useless, she thought. So she printed her summary notes at the stationery shop and kept a torch on the desk. And if I'm ill for two days? Then everything shifts and I panic. So she left Sunday afternoons blank and labelled them "catch-up". In the second week her brother Farhan came home with a fever, and two days later so did she. She rested, then used the Sunday slot and one lighter evening to cover the missed chapters. The plan bent, but didn't break.

qa.q: What did Preeti label Sunday afternoons?
How might Preeti have felt when she caught the fever?
qa.a: She may have felt frustrated and worried at first, but less panicked, knowing a catch-up slot was waiting.

qa.q: What other disruption could Preeti plan for?
qa.a: A family event or a change in exam dates, by keeping a second light day in the last week as extra slack.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel when his sister falls ill too?
qa.a: Farhan may feel guilty for bringing the fever home, and relieved that her plan had room for it.

grounding: Shows a student expecting summer power cuts and fevers, printing notes and keeping a spare Sunday slot so one disruption doesn't derail revision.

subtype: Approach: contingency planning for illness or power cuts [Thinking]
passage: In the Chennai flat, Seema's desk had two things her friends found old-fashioned: a thick file of printed notes and a battery lantern. "Everything's on your phone," her neighbour Abhinav said, flipping through. "What's the paper for?" "Summer," Seema said. She had thought it through in March: every summer the power went for hours, and the phone died with it. Every summer someone in the building caught a viral fever. So the notes were printed, and every Sunday from two to six was an empty slot on her calendar, marked "spare". In the second week of May a storm knocked out the power for a whole evening. The building went dark. Seema lit the lantern, opened the file at Chemistry and kept going. The chapter she didn't finish went into Sunday's spare slot.

qa.q: What time was Seema's spare Sunday slot?
How did Seema feel when the building went dark?
qa.a: She seemed calm and prepared, lighting the lantern and carrying on rather than panicking 🙂.

qa.q: Why did the spare Sunday slot matter?
qa.a: It gave the unfinished chapter a place to go, so one disrupted evening didn't push the whole schedule back.

qa.q: How might Abhinav see the printed file now?
qa.a: Abhinav, who thought it old-fashioned, might see it differently after the storm evening.

grounding: Shows a student who planned for power cuts and fevers with printed notes and a spare Sunday slot, so a storm doesn't derail the plan.
